[Part 3](../problems/unintended-prior.qmd) read the Gamma(1.60, 1.22) hyperprior of
paper Figure 1 through two formulas. Here the same prior runs as a process. Each
restaurant draws its own alpha from Gamma(1.60, 1.22), then seats J = 50 customers by the
[Chinese restaurant rule](../dpm/crp.qmd): an occupied table with probability proportional
to its size, a new table with probability proportional to alpha. The widget repeats this
for 1000 restaurants.


## What the restaurants say

- **About five tables.** The table counts pile up around five; the dots are the exact
  prior pmf of K_50 (mean 5.05), and with seed 1 the 1000 restaurants average 5.04 tables.
- **One table often seats most of the room.** In about 63% of the restaurants the largest
  table holds more than 25 of the 50 customers. The analyst asked for "about five
  clusters" and also got, without asking, a prior in which one cluster usually dominates.
- **Two probabilities, two questions.** Pr(W_SB > .5) = .487 asks whether the table of a
  *randomly chosen customer* holds more than half of the population. Pr(W_max > .5) = .636
  asks whether the *largest* table does. The second is always at least the first
  (Proposition 1 of the paper bounds it between S(.5) and 2 S(.5)); the red share in the
  simulation estimates a 50-customer version of it.

Press **Simulate 1000 restaurants** (or Enter) for a new seed, hover over the wall of
squares to open one restaurant, or move a and b: at Gamma(1, 3) most restaurants have one
or two tables and the red squares take over.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
These are prior statements: no data have been seen. K_J is the number of fitted
components (occupied clusters) among the J units.
:::
